statement.capacity_retry.departs: A20 (at most five continuations a conversation in 24 hours, at least 15 minutes apart), A21 (the attempt, no-progress and continuation budgets), A22 (waits come only from the retry timing you chose) and B9 (only a failure's kind is kept: this also reads Codex's own error code, never its words).
statement.capacity_retry.does: When Codex says it is at capacity (its own error code serverOverloaded), it tries again sooner and more often than the standard edition: about a minute after the failure, then two, four and five minutes, each lengthened by up to a fifth, at least a minute apart and at most 48 times a day in one conversation. It keeps this up for as long as you choose, one to twelve hours (two by default), counted on the clock from the first failure, whatever it waited for meanwhile; after that the standard edition's own limits apply again, and they may end the task. Each try is the ordinary continuation through Codex's queue command, with its marker. Other server errors, rate limits and usage limits keep the standard edition's waits.
statement.capacity_retry.instead: The standard edition waits as its retry timing says, sends at most five continuations to a conversation in any 24 hours, at least 15 minutes apart, and stops a task after four attempts, three in a row with no progress, or six continuations.
statement.capacity_retry.risks: Retrying a busy service often adds to its load and spends your usage on continuations that may fail again, and each try is a visible message in the conversation. All advanced features together still send at most 12 times an hour; while that limit is reached, capacity errors are handled as the standard edition handles them, which may end the task. A continuation whose delivery cannot be proven is never sent again, and this feature turns itself off.
statement.capacity_retry.stop: Turn it off in the Dashboard, or turn every advanced feature off; capacity errors then wait as the standard edition makes them wait. Cancel a waiting recovery to stop that one.
statement.goal_continuation.departs: 0.5 (the product never changes a goal's state), A2 (continuations go through one channel only, Codex's queue command), A11 (nothing is done for a conversation the app does not have open), B3 (Codex's state changes only through its queue and plugin commands) and B4 (the app server is asked only for usage and to take back a queued message).
statement.goal_continuation.does: When a usage limit paused a conversation's Codex goal, and the conversation is due to continue while the Codex app does not have it open, it sets that goal active again through Codex's own app server, so Codex carries the goal on when the app next opens the conversation. It resumes only a goal that exists and was paused by the usage limit; it never creates a goal and never reads or changes what the goal says. While the app has the conversation open, the continuation goes through Codex's queue as in the standard edition, with the goal set active first only where measurement M2b passed for your version of Codex.
statement.goal_continuation.instead: The standard edition never touches a goal. It waits until the app has the conversation open and then queues its continuation with Codex's queue command; a goal paused by the usage limit stays paused until you resume it yourself.
statement.goal_continuation.risks: Measurement M2 found that a goal set this way is not seen while the app has the conversation open, and is picked up once the app opens it again; that is why it acts only on a conversation the app does not have open. Another version of Codex may handle goals differently. When the result cannot be confirmed - Codex does not answer, or the goal does not read back as resumed - that interruption is never tried again and this feature turns itself off. While a goal is carrying the conversation on, the standard continuation waits for up to ten minutes after the app opens it, so the two do not both run. Every recovery gate, limit and pause still applies.
statement.goal_continuation.stop: Turn it off in the Dashboard, or turn off every advanced feature at once; continuations then go only through Codex's queue again. A goal it already set active stays active: pause the goal in Codex if you want it to stop.
statement.marker_free_continuation.depar: A2 (continuations go through one channel only, Codex's queue command), A4 (each continuation carries its marker, and it counts as delivered only when that marker is found), B3 (Codex's state changes only through its queue and plugin commands) and B4 (the app server is asked only for usage and to take back a queued message).
statement.marker_free_continuation.does: Sends each continuation without the marker the standard edition ends it with. The message is added to the conversation's queue through Codex's own app server, under an id made from the interruption, and that id - which Codex keeps on the message - is what proves it arrived. Past its daily limits, a continuation goes with the marker, as in the standard edition.
statement.marker_free_continuation.inste: The standard edition sends every continuation through Codex's queue command and ends it with a short marker, [codex-auto-resume:…], which is how it finds its own message in the conversation afterwards.
statement.marker_free_continuation.risks: It rests on an app-server request measured on one version of Codex (M7); another version may refuse it or stop keeping the id. When arrival cannot be proven - the app server refuses or does not answer, or the message never shows - the continuation is treated as uncertain, exactly as the standard edition treats one: it is never sent again, and this feature turns itself off. Every recovery gate and limit stays as it is.
statement.marker_free_continuation.stop: Turn it off in the Dashboard, or turn off every advanced feature at once; continuations then go through Codex's queue command with the marker again. One already sent without a marker is still followed by its id to the end.
statement.start_with_codex.departs: C4 (the product starts nothing on its own when Codex starts) and F6 (it adds one process-creation route, through WMI, beyond the ones the standard edition uses).
statement.start_with_codex.does: Starts the watcher when Codex starts, even inside the job Codex closes when it quits. With this on and no watcher running, it asks Windows (WMI) to start the watcher outside that job, so it keeps running after Codex closes. It registers nothing.
statement.start_with_codex.instead: The standard edition starts nothing here: where Codex would end the watcher it writes one line to say so and waits for you to start the watcher yourself once Codex has closed.
statement.start_with_codex.risks: Its only purpose is to leave a limit Codex places on its plugins on purpose. If WMI is off, or a policy blocks process creation through it, nothing starts and the reason is logged; you are never asked to change that policy. It starts the watcher and nothing else, keeps every recovery gate, and never starts a second copy.
statement.start_with_codex.stop: Turn it off in the Dashboard, or turn off every advanced feature at once. It never starts a second watcher while one is running, and it only ever starts this installation's own launcher.
statement.structured_rules.departs: 0.5 (unknown failures are never retried), A13 (only the classified kinds are recovered), A14 (anything unclassified is never retried), A26 (continuation text only for a kind that is recovered) and B9 (only a failure's kind is kept, never Codex's error code).
statement.structured_rules.does: Lets you write up to ten rules in the Dashboard. Each names one of Codex's own error codes, and if you like a range of status numbers, and the kind of temporary failure to treat it as: a dropped connection, a timeout, a rate limit, a server error or a broken stream. A rule applies only to a failure the product could not classify; it then waits as that kind waits in your retry timing, counts against that kind's budget and follows that kind's switch in Settings. A code the product already knows can never be a rule, nor one whose name speaks of a policy, budget, quota, permission, approval, sign-in or cancellation, and no rule makes a failure a usage limit. Rules read codes, never the words of an error. It takes up only failures from the last hour, and none from before it was turned on.
statement.structured_rules.instead: The standard edition never retries a failure it cannot classify, and nothing you set can change that.
statement.structured_rules.risks: A rule is your judgement that a code is temporary. A wrong one retries failures that retrying cannot fix, until that kind's budget runs out, and Codex may rename or reuse a code in another version. The continuation is the short standard message.
statement.structured_rules.stop: Remove the rule, turn the feature off or set it to watch only in the Dashboard, or turn every advanced feature off. A recovery a rule took up and has not sent then ends without being sent.
statement.unknown_failure_budget.departs: 0.5 (unknown failures are never retried), A13 (only the classified kinds are recovered), A14 (anything unclassified is never retried), A26 (continuation text only for a kind that is recovered), B9 (only a failure's kind is kept, never Codex's error code) and D2 (state holds only the product's own fixed words, never a code Codex chose).
statement.unknown_failure_budget.does: When a turn fails with an error code of Codex's that the product cannot classify, it continues the conversation anyway, on a budget of its own: one to three tries a task, as you choose (one by default), at most three a day in one conversation, the first ten minutes after the failure, then 15 and 30. It never takes up a failure that came with no code, or a code whose name speaks of a policy, budget, quota, permission, approval, sign-in or cancellation. Each failure it takes up leaves a sample on this PC: Codex's error code, the status number, how many items of each kind the turn left, when it failed and how long it ran - never a word of the error, the conversation or the reply. You see the samples here, and a diagnostics export you ask for includes them; nothing sends them. It takes up only failures from the last hour, and none from before it was turned on.
statement.unknown_failure_budget.instead: The standard edition never retries a failure it cannot classify: the conversation waits for you.
statement.unknown_failure_budget.risks: A failure nobody classified may be one retrying cannot help, or one where trying again repeats something a person should have decided; Codex continues from the short standard message. A sample keeps an error code Codex chose, which may say more than the product's own words. A continuation whose delivery cannot be proven is never sent again, and this feature turns itself off.
statement.unknown_failure_budget.stop: Turn it off or set it to watch only in the Dashboard, or turn every advanced feature off; a recovery it was waiting to send then ends without being sent. Samples are kept 90 days at most.
